common_name: David Auyong Chaconia (Double Chaconia, Trinidad's National Flower)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or layered stock in spring in humid, well-drained tropical soil; this is a vegetatively propagated clone that does not reliably reproduce its double bracts from seed.

directions: David Auyong is a double-bracted selection of chaconia, the national flower of Trinidad and Tobago, traced back to cuttings taken from a single wild plant discovered on the island in 1957 and selected for carrying two whorls of scarlet bracts instead of the single ring typical of the species. Grow it as a large, open-canopied flowering shrub or small tree in humid lowland gardens, leaving room for the long, arching flower spikes to display without crowding from neighboring plants. Established plants tolerate the dappled light of a forest-edge or second-growth planting site but produce the heaviest bloom with several hours of direct sun and consistent rainfall or irrigation. Because the double form is a selected clone, propagate only from rooted cuttings or layering rather than from seed.
sources: National Trust of Trinidad and Tobago

common_name: Moruga Hill Rice (Trinidad Merikin Heirloom Upland Rice)

planting.note: Direct sow into warm, well-drained garden or field soil after danger of frost has passed; unlike paddy rice this dry-land type is grown on raised ground without standing water.

directions: Moruga Hill Rice is a dry-land upland rice landrace carried to Trinidad's Moruga district in the early 1800s by the Merikins, formerly enslaved African American soldiers who settled the Company Villages of south Trinidad after serving with the British in the War of 1812. It is sown directly into ordinary field or garden soil rather than a flooded paddy, relying on seasonal rainfall or routine irrigation to bring the crop through to harvest, and shows good tolerance of the thinner, less fertile soils typical of the Moruga hills. The grain has a nutty flavor that distinguishes it from standard milled white rice. Harvest by hand once the lower leaves yellow and the drooping seed heads turn golden-brown, then dry the cut panicles thoroughly before threshing and milling.
